Sampled HR@10 against 99 negatives measures success within that candidate set; it does not estimate full-catalog HR@10 directly. Krichene and Rendle show sampled metrics can reverse model comparisons even in expectation. Preserve the pinned users, candidates, seeds and evaluator; describe conclusions as benchmark-specific. Fixed candidates improve paired comparability but do not remove sampling bias. [On Sampled Metrics](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)

Recommended uncertainty protocol: retain each user’s binary hit for both models; bootstrap paired users with replacement within each category, keeping their candidates fixed. For each replicate, calculate the four category HR differences and their equal-weight macro-average; report the observed difference and a 95% percentile interval. This estimates user-sampling uncertainty conditional on the fitted models and candidate sets, excluding training-seed and candidate-sampling variability. Repeated validation selection creates optimism; an ordinary bootstrap interval does not correct the winner’s selection bias. Record all trials, avoid interpreting tiny selected gains as confirmed improvements, and reserve final claims for the host’s untouched held-out evaluation. [Selection Bias](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v11/cawley10a.html)

Recommended shortcut audit: predefine training-only item-popularity bands and user-history-length bands; report counts, HR@10 and paired gains within each, alongside category results. Inspect whether gains concentrate on popular targets or particular history lengths. History-order shuffling or truncation can provide inference-only sensitivity diagnostics for the same trained GRU, without fitting or fusing additional predictors. Such audits flag possible shortcuts, not causal proof; exposure and popularity biases can reward reproducing logged-data patterns. [Offline Evaluation Challenges](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/aaai.12051)
